content: A group, also referred to as a family, in the periodic table of chemical elements is a vertical column. The standard periodic table consists of 18 groups. The modern understanding of the periodic table's structure is based on the fact that elements within the same group share similar configurations of their outermost electron shells. This similarity in electron configuration is significant because the chemical properties of elements are largely determined by the arrangement of their outermost electrons. There are three distinct methods for numbering the groups in the periodic table. One system uses Hindu-Arabic numerals, while the other two employ Roman numerals. The Roman numeral system represents the traditional naming convention for groups, whereas the Arabic numeral system is the one recommended by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC). The IUPAC introduced this system to replace the older naming conventions in an effort to minimize the confusion caused by the coexistence of two older, yet conflicting, systems. The two older systems, known as the old IUPAC system and the CAS (Chemical Abstracts Service) system, combined Roman numerals with letters, leading to significant confusion. In the old IUPAC system, the letters A and B were used to designate the left (A) and right (B) sections of the periodic table. In contrast, the CAS system used A to denote main group elements and B to represent transition elements. The old IUPAC system was predominantly used in Europe, while the CAS system was more commonly adopted in America. To address the inconsistencies and confusion caused by these two systems, the new IUPAC scheme was developed. This modern system was designed to unify the naming conventions and eliminate the ambiguity that arose from the use of identical names to signify different concepts in the older systems.
